UNE COM · OMS-1 Psychiatry Block · Lecture Notes

Personality Disorders

Ryan Smith, DO, PhD — "Personality Disorders 2026"
Topics10 PDs across 3 clusters
Core ModelEgo-syntonic, pervasive, inflexible, onset ≤ adolescence
Boards FactThese are mostly first-order "what's the diagnosis" questions
High-YieldZero FDA-approved meds for any PD · DBT for BPD specifically
Yield check: Dr. Smith's framing for this whole topic: personality disorders are ego-syntonic — the patient sees no conflict between themselves and the world ("the world is the problem, not them"), which is exactly why they're pervasive, inflexible, and rarely self-present for treatment. Because effective treatments are so limited, boards questions here are overwhelmingly "what's the most likely diagnosis" rather than treatment questions — so the emphasis below is on crisp, memorable differentiation between the 10 disorders.
Section 01

Foundations: Trait vs. Disorder, Ego-Syntonic vs. Ego-Dystonic ⭐ HY

Personality Trait

DefinitionAn enduring, repetitive pattern of perceiving, relating to, and thinking about the environment and oneself.
Key pointEveryone has traits — a little paranoid, a little obsessive, a little dependent. None of these are disorders on their own; they're variations of normal, and they're what make people interesting. The problem is when a cluster of these traits comes together and causes real impairment — that's when it becomes a disorder.

Personality Disorder

DefinitionA pervasive, inflexible, maladaptive manner of viewing the world, originating in adolescence or earlier (some sources trace it to the first 2 years of life) — never developing fresh at, say, age 50 (though it can be missed until then).
The 3 words to knowPervasive — present across all areas of life, not situational like ADHD. Inflexible — extremely difficult to change or treat. Maladaptive — goes against social norms.
🎙️
The "blue wall" analogy: "This wall is blue. How long do you think it would take me to convince you that this wall is red? A hell of a long time. That's about the level you have to think about when treating a patient with a personality disorder to get some motion on improving their condition. It's almost like you have to reprogram their brain." Dr. Smith also frames it as colored glasses: the patient sees the entire world through a lens shaped by their personality development — and only they can see that color. Everything they perceive is filtered through it, so from their point of view, the world is the problem, not them. They can't understand why the world won't conform to their expectations, because what they see doesn't match what everyone else is seeing.

Ego-Syntonic vs. Ego-Dystonic ⭐ HY

Most Psychiatric DisordersPersonality Disorders
TermEgo-dystonicEgo-syntonic
Relationship to selfConflict between the person and the world — e.g., a depressed patient knows they're depressed and wants it to changeNo conflict between the person and how they view the world — the way they see things feels perfectly fine to them
InsightPresent — the person is "aware" of their conditionAbsent — the person is "unaware," and often feels persecuted by a world that won't conform to them
Care-seekingSelf-presents for treatmentRarely self-presents; usually brought in by someone else, or presents for a single symptom without seeing the larger pattern
🕵️
How you actually make the diagnosis: since these patients rarely complain of ego-syntonic problems, the diagnosis has to be pulled out through collateral history — a spouse, sibling, or longtime friend who can confirm the pattern has been present since childhood/adolescence ("Oh yeah, he was like this when he was 7 or 8"). That longstanding timeline is also a key differentiator from a primary psychotic disorder, which typically has a more identifiable onset.
📌
Genetics + environment: personality disorders have both a real heritable/genetic component and an environmental component — twin studies show the genetic predisposition can be present without being expressed unless an environmental trigger "fuels" it.
Section 02

DSM-5 General Personality Disorder Criteria & The 3 Clusters ⭐ HY

The general template every specific personality disorder is built on top of

CriterionRequirement
AAn enduring pattern of inner experience/behavior deviating markedly from cultural expectations, in ≥2 of: cognition, affectivity, interpersonal functioning, impulse control
BInflexible and pervasive across a broad range of personal/social situations
CClinically significant distress or impairment (social, occupational, other)
DStable, long duration, traceable to adolescence or early adulthood
ENot better explained by another mental disorder
FNot attributable to a substance or another medical condition (e.g., head trauma)
💊
Treatment reality check, up front: personality disorders are among the most difficult diagnoses to treat in psychiatry — there is no FDA-approved medication for any of the 10, and there's no single core psychotherapy across the board (the one exception: dialectical behavioral therapy, DBT, was developed specifically for borderline PD — Section 13). Off-label medications exist to target specific symptoms (depression, paranoia, irritability) that arise from the disorder, not the disorder itself.

The 3 Clusters ⭐ HY

Cluster A — "Weird, Wacky"

Odd & eccentric
MembersParanoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal

Cluster B — "Wild"

Dramatic, emotional, erratic
MembersAntisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic

Cluster C — "Worried"

Anxious & fearful
MembersDependent, Obsessive-Compulsive, Avoidant
🧠
Cluster mnemonic: "Weird, Wild, and Worried" — A is weird/eccentric, B is wild/dramatic, C is worried/anxious. Each cluster (as you'll see in Sections 05, 09, and 12) shares a common underlying theme: Cluster A overlaps with negative symptoms of schizophrenia, Cluster B centers on affective instability/impulsivity, and Cluster C centers on anxious symptomatology.

Section 03 · Cluster A

Paranoid Personality Disorder

Paranoid PD

Intense distrust from assuming others' motives are malicious
Core picturePreoccupation with unjustified doubts leads the person to perceive even innocuous interactions as character assassination — producing extreme suspicion and strained, stilted interpersonal relationships. In group/work settings, this drives job dissatisfaction and difficulty maintaining employment.
Watch forOften confused with features of a true psychotic disorder — but there's no frank psychosis here, just a pervasive characterological suspicion.

Mnemonic: GET FACT

LetterCriterion
GGrudges held for long periods
EExploitation expected (without sufficient basis)
TTrustworthiness of others doubted
FFidelity of sexual partner questioned
AAttacks on character are perceived (and thought true)
CConfides in others rarely, if at all
TThreatening meanings read into events
🎙️
The delusional-disorder overlap: patients with paranoid PD can present a lot like delusional disorder, jealous type — convinced their partner is cheating "despite all the evidence you can give them." The difference is degree and structure: paranoid PD is a pervasive characterological stance across all relationships, not a single fixed, encapsulated delusion.
▶ Paranoid personality disorder case 🔒 UNE
Section 04 · Cluster A

Schizoid Personality Disorder

Schizoid PD

Blunted affect, detachment, and a genuine preference for solitude
Core pictureBlunted affect (restrained emotionality — e.g., finding out you won $57 million and responding "Oh yeah, that's great") associated with feelings of detachment; relationships are wanted to be distant, and solitude is actively preferred, not just tolerated. Comes across as emotionally cold, though that's often just the flat presentation rather than genuine coldness underneath.
The classic image"Think of the night watchman" — a quiet campus job with minimal social interaction is genuinely ideal for this presentation, not a compromise. These patients may have one or two sexual partners in a lifetime, or none — "asexual" gets applied colloquially, though that's technically a misnomer; it's more that sexual/romantic interaction with others just isn't of interest.
Social patternMay have one or two close friends who are similarly solitary/reclusive — they can identify with people who see the world the same way.

Mnemonic: SIR SAFE

LetterCriterion
SSolitary lifestyle
IIndifferent to praise or criticism
RRelationships of no interest
SSexual experiences not of interest
AActivities not enjoyed
FFriends lacking
EEmotionally cold and detached
🎙️
Real patient, Eastport, Maine: "I had a patient who talked like it was 1850 — this very old-English way of talking. Rather than saying 'what's that,' she'd say something like 'whatever have you in your hands.' It was the most bizarre thing I've ever seen." (This particular patient actually had schizotypal PD, not schizoid — her odd speech pattern is used in Section 05 — but it's a good illustration of how idiosyncratic presentation can be within Cluster A.)
🎬
Video vignette: a 45-year-old man who lost his tech-supervisor job of 27 years "to a computer" describes his home life: he lives alone, except for a stray dog that's taken to eating meals at his house. Asked the dog's name, he says: "He's just there." He can't even bring himself to name a dog he feeds daily — a vivid illustration of blunted affect and detachment. Note the brief hesitation when asked about living alone: it's not that solitude itself troubles him, it's the discomfort of having to explain and be judged for it by others.
🧠
Schizoid vs. Avoidant — the classic mix-up: both isolate, but for opposite reasons. Schizoid PD patients isolate because they genuinely prefer solitude and have no interest in relationships. Avoidant PD patients (Section 10) want connection but avoid it out of fear of rejection/ridicule. Full contrast table in Section 10.
▶ Schizoid personality disorder case 🔒 UNE
Section 05 · Cluster A

Schizotypal Personality Disorder ⭐ HY

Schizotypal PD

The Cluster A member most associated with true psychotic illness
Core pictureDifficulty interacting with others driven by discomfort with the act of interacting itself — critically, not from negative self-image (contrast with avoidant PD, Section 10). May demonstrate cognitive distortions, odd speech patterns, and genuinely strange perceptual experiences (believing they can see the future, read minds, sense energy, etc.) that influence behavior.
The headline featureUnusual perceptions — this is the discriminating symptom to focus on. The affect can be inappropriate to context (e.g., unexpectedly cheerful at a somber occasion), and ideas of reference are common (believing the TV or environment is sending them personal messages).

Mnemonic: UFO AIDER — fittingly, given the supernatural/paranormal flavor of many of these beliefs

LetterCriterion
UUnusual perceptions
FFriendless except for family
OOdd beliefs, thinking, and speech
AAffect — inappropriate, constricted
IIdeas of reference
DDoubts others — suspicious
EEccentric — appearance/behavior
RReluctant in social situations, anxious
🎙️
Real patient, Eastport, Maine: a patient who spoke as if it were the 1850s — an old-English speaking style ("whatever have you in your hands" instead of "what's that") — the odd-speech-pattern criterion in vivid form. She also kept a crystal ball and wore mismatched socks. Critically: she believed she looked completely normal — there was no negative self-image at all, just a strange (to everyone else) but internally-consistent way of experiencing the world. Family described her as "a great lady, but a little strange" — and loved her anyway. That's the friendless-except-for-family pattern in action.
🎬
Video vignette — library worker: recently moved from the back room to the front desk, he explains he doesn't make small talk with coworkers: "I've always been a Pluto — up beyond the rest, circling on the fringe, ever watching, and seeing more in the darkness than the rest." He also senses (with no objective basis) that his supervisor and customers are unhappy with him, and believes coworkers can "feel what he's feeling" when he thinks about depressing books — so he eats lunch alone to avoid "ruining their meal." The trigger for his current distress: being moved to a public-facing role, forcing more interaction than he's comfortable with.
📌
Boards-relevant fact: schizotypal PD is the one personality disorder most associated with true psychotic disorders — it can coexist with schizophrenia, and the symptom overlap means it's sometimes misdiagnosed as (or mistaken for) a primary psychotic illness.

Cluster A Summary

All three Cluster A disorders share an underlying overlap with the negative symptoms of schizophrenia — social withdrawal, reclusiveness, restricted affect

▶ Schizotypal personality disorder case 🔒 UNE
Section 06 · Cluster B

Antisocial Personality Disorder

Antisocial PD

"Sociopath" / "psychopathic behavior" / "psychopathy" in lay terms
Core pictureA pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of others' rights — impulsive, disregarding the safety/welfare of others and themselves, failing to conform to social norms, engaging in unlawful activity, and lacking remorse. Strongly male-predominant (~3:1 or higher).
Classic quote patternA man with several children by several women, when asked about supporting them, responds: "Well, I didn't give birth to them — it's not my responsibility." Complete detachment from the reality of the situation, with instant rationalization/externalization of blame.

Mnemonic: CALLOUS MAN

LetterCriterion
CConduct disorder before age 15y; current age at least 18y
AAntisocial acts — commits acts that are grounds for arrest
LLies frequently
LLacunae — lacks a superego
OObligations not honored
UUnstable — can't plan ahead
SSafety of self and others ignored
MMoney problems — spouse/children not supported
AAggressive, assaultive
NNot occurring exclusively during schizophrenia or mania (exclusion criterion)
📌
The conduct disorder link is required, not incidental: DSM-5 requires documentation of conduct disorder before age 15 to diagnose antisocial PD — this is one of the only personality disorders with an explicit childhood-diagnosis prerequisite built into the criteria (most PDs are simply never diagnosed in children, but this one specifically requires evidence of it). Conduct disorder is essentially "antisocial PD in a child" — harming animals, lack of remorse, violating others' rights — and typically (though not always documented) precedes the adult diagnosis.
🎬
Video vignette: the visual introduction alone tells most of the story — smoking, a motorcycle in the background, a lamp shaped like a naked woman. A "wild guy" aesthetic that reinforces the impulsivity/disregard-for-norms theme before the patient even speaks.
▶ Antisocial personality disorder case 🔒 UNE
Section 07 · Cluster B

Borderline Personality Disorder ⭐ HY — "the one you need to know the most"

Borderline PD

Instability in self-image and interpersonal relationships
Name origin"Borderline" of depression and psychosis — patients oscillate near the boundary between mood dysregulation and brief, stress-related psychotic phenomena (see micropsychotic episodes below).
Core pictureImpulsivity that may lead to self-harm (drug abuse, promiscuity, cutting), and relationships that are polarized — black/white, love/hate — in a pattern of extreme idealization followed by devaluation. Drives frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment, alongside chronic feelings of emptiness.
F > MRoughly 3:1 — the one Cluster B disorder that's female-predominant.

Mnemonic: I RAISED A PAIN

LetterCriterion
IIdentity disturbance
RRelationships are unstable
AAbandonment frantically avoided (whether real or imagined)
IImpulsivity
SSuicidal gestures (threats, self-mutilation, etc.)
EEmptiness
DDissociative symptoms
AAffective instability
PParanoid ideation (stress-related and transient)
AAnger is poorly controlled
IIdealization followed by devaluation ("splitting")
NNegativistic — undermines themselves with self-defeating behavior

Self-Harm in BPD: It's About Pain, Not Death ⭐ HY

💡
Cutting (classically wrists or thighs), head-banging, or burning with cigarettes — the goal in the vast majority of cases is not suicide. It's to generate physical pain that distracts from unbearable emotional pain (the same underlying logic as trichotillomania's hair-pulling as anxiety distraction). If a patient with BPD does die by suicide, it's typically accidental — e.g., someone overdoses on pills and calls their boyfriend to be "rescued" as part of the pattern, and if he's delayed by traffic and doesn't arrive in time, death results from a gesture that was never actually intended to be lethal.
🧠
Para-suicidal behavior — behavior that looks like self-harm/suicide on the surface, but isn't intended to end in death; the intent is to feel physical pain, or to get someone else to notice, acknowledge, and support them. Dr. Smith's memory hook, straight from organic chemistry: para- as in para-dimethylbenzene means "opposite" — para-suicidal is, functionally, the opposite of suicidal, even though it can look identical from the outside.
The "Condiment Patient" — a 3-part story on abandonment avoidance

A patient worked at a restaurant 20 miles from home, living with a boyfriend roughly 20 years her junior who mooched off her, drank all day, and repeatedly cheated on her. She'd installed a tracking device on his phone, and whenever he left the house to meet another woman, she would drop everything at work and drive to find him.

Part 1: She tracks him to a woman's apartment, bangs on the door with her fists, and when the woman who answers offers her a hammer instead of a key, she uses it to break down the upstairs apartment door, drags the other woman out by the hair, and beats her on the front lawn — while the boyfriend simply drives away. She isn't angry at him; she's furious at the woman "stealing" him.

Part 2: He cheats again. She drives to a different house, finds a ladder outside, climbs to a second-floor window, and bangs on the glass — until someone inside shoves the ladder away from the house and she falls.

Part 3: Wanting to get back at the other woman directly, she strips her own bed, squirts ketchup, mustard, and mayonnaise all over the sheets, remakes the bed neatly, and hides outside waiting for the couple to arrive at her house. Once they're inside, she comes in with a blowtorch and sets her own bed on fire with them in it — the resulting smoke was serious enough that a baby in the apartment above required treatment for smoke inhalation.

🎯
Why this is the teaching case for abandonment avoidance: at every step, her rage is directed at the "other woman," never meaningfully at the boyfriend who is actually cheating and mooching off her. The underlying driver isn't really about him being wronged — it's the terror of losing him, any way that happens, however bad the relationship is. She ultimately faced legal consequences (harassment/stalking charges) that did nothing to fix the actual problem: a bad relationship she couldn't leave because of the abandonment fear underneath it all. "Even though the relationship is unstable and it's a bad relationship, avoidance of the abandonment is the critical key piece here."

Dissociation & Micropsychotic Episodes ⭐ HY

📌
BPD belongs on your differential for psychosis: under acute stress, patients can have brief micropsychotic episodes and dissociative symptoms — doing things during a period of time they later don't remember. This is the literal meaning behind the name "borderline": the patient sits at the boundary between mood dysregulation and transient psychosis.
💬
Ask directly: "Do you feel empty inside?" Patients with BPD will often answer with exactly that phrase — "I feel empty inside. I feel like I don't have a purpose. I feel like I don't know who I am." Asked about their purpose in life, the answer is invariably some version of "I have no idea" — day-to-day survival of the emotionality, rather than any coherent long-term direction.
🧠
Borderline PD vs. Bipolar Disorder — a frequently confused pair, in both directions: always keep bipolar disorder on the differential when BPD is suspected, and vice versa. The key discriminator is timescale and trigger: bipolar mood episodes last days-to-weeks and shift relatively independent of external events; BPD's affective instability is reactive — it shifts rapidly (hours) in direct response to interpersonal triggers (a perceived slight, a fear of abandonment), and is embedded in the broader identity-disturbance/relationship-instability picture rather than existing as a standalone mood episode.
Video vignette — "Mr. Rice"

A well-groomed man carrying a bag that says "Believe," on crutches, presenting after being seen at a medical clinic for a wrist infection. He describes the medical team as "totally inept" for not knowing amoxicillin cross-reacts with a penicillin allergy — and is already planning a lawsuit, despite not yet having spoken to a lawyer. Asked about the wrist injury: he broke a fraternity house window and cut himself while drinking at a party. He's 40 years old and describes himself as an "honorary member" of the fraternity — having met the group at a bar, been made to feel like their best friend, invited to move in, and then, predictably, left out and disappointed once the novelty wore off.

🎯
What to notice: the instant idealization-then-devaluation pattern applied to the medical team ("inept," already litigious) mirrors the same splitting seen in his account of the fraternity — intense idealization of a new relationship, followed swiftly by disappointment/devaluation once reality doesn't match the fantasy. The age-inappropriate desire to be an "honorary" fraternity member also speaks to the identity disturbance and instability criteria.
▶ Borderline personality disorder case 🔒 UNE
Section 08 · Cluster B

Histrionic Personality Disorder

Histrionic PD

Emotionality and attention-seeking
Core pictureNot happy unless they're the center of attention. To gain attention, patients are easily swayed by fads, overly trusting, and may interact in inappropriately sexual ways. Displays of emotion are theatrical and overly dramatic — yet superficial, and can shift instantly.
EpidemiologyM = F, 2–3% prevalence — one of the more common personality disorders, and (unlike most of Cluster B) not sex-skewed.

Mnemonic: I CRAVE SIN

LetterCriterion
IInappropriate behavior — seductive or provocative
CCenter of attention
RRelationships are seen as closer than they really are
AAppearance is most important
VVulnerable to others' suggestions
EEmotional expression is exaggerated
SShifting emotions, shallow
IImpressionistic manner of speaking (lacks detail)
NNovelty is craved
🎙️
Dr. Smith references a memorable "sea glass" patient story for this disorder in lecture — worth asking about directly if you weren't in the room for it, since the full narrative isn't captured in these notes.

Section 09 · Cluster B

Narcissistic Personality Disorder

Narcissistic PD

Grandiosity and a need for admiration
Core pictureProne to grandiose fantasies (unlimited success, brilliance, power), with a persistent need for admiration. Generally lacking empathy; arrogant; a pervasive sense of entitlement. Expects others to acknowledge their supposed superiority and feels disproportionately jealous or threatened when others receive praise.
Epidemiology<1% prevalence, M > F.

Mnemonic: A FAME GAME

LetterCriterion
AAdmiration required in excessive amounts
FFantasizes about unlimited success, brilliance, etc.
AArrogant
MManipulative
EEnvious of others
GGrandiose sense of importance
AAssociates with special people
MMe-first attitude
EEmpathy lacking for others
▶ Narcissistic personality disorder case 🔒 UNE

Cluster B Summary — Two Axes

All four Cluster B disorders plotted on axes of affective instability (vertical) and impulsivity (horizontal) — borderline sits at the intersection of both being highest; histrionic leans toward affective instability; antisocial leans toward impulsivity; narcissistic sits comparatively lower on both

Section 10 · Cluster C

Avoidant Personality Disorder ⭐ HY

Avoidant PD

They want friends — they just don't know how to get them
Core pictureDysfunction in interpersonal functioning driven by discomfort and self-inadequacy. Because of fear of shame, ridicule, or rejection, patients interact with others as little as possible; new activities are rarely attempted, and new relationships are seldom formed.

Mnemonic: RIDICULE

LetterCriterion
RRestrained within relationships
IInhibited in interpersonal situations
DDisapproval expected at work
IInadequate (view of self)
CCriticism is expected in social situations
UUnwilling to get involved
LLongs for attachment to others
EEmbarrassment is the feared emotion

Schizoid vs. Avoidant — Know This Distinction Cold ⭐ HY

SchizoidAvoidant
Do they want relationships?No — genuine preference for solitudeYes — they want friends and connection
Why do they isolate?Indifference — relationships hold no interestFear — of shame, ridicule, or rejection
Self-imageNot driven by negative self-imageDriven by self-inadequacy
Response to praise/criticismIndifferent either wayHighly sensitive to both

Section 11 · Cluster C

Dependent Personality Disorder

Dependent PD

Excessively clingy, with a pervasive need to be cared for
Core pictureProne to separation anxiety; jumps from relationship to relationship as soon as one ends, rather than tolerating time alone. Trouble making everyday decisions independently, and goes out of their way to hand responsibility for major life decisions to someone else.

Mnemonic: DARN HURT

LetterCriterion
DDisagreement is difficult to express
AAdvice — needs excessive input
RResponsibility for major areas delegated to others
NNurturance — seeks an excessive degree from others
HHelpless when alone
UUnrealistically preoccupied with being left to care for self
RRelationships desperately sought (when an established one ends)
TTasks — has difficulty initiating projects
🎙️
The "serpent around the brain" patient — likely a familiar callback: Dr. Smith references a "serpent around brain" patient story for dependent PD in lecture. This is almost certainly the same patient discussed under delusional disorder, somatic type, in the psychotic disorders unit — a woman with a decades-long somatic delusion of a snake coiled around her brain, whose headaches were ultimately traced to undiagnosed opiate withdrawal, and who Dr. Smith followed for 3–4 years afterward. If so, the callback here is to a different facet of the same patient: beyond the somatic delusion itself, her intense, prolonged reliance on her physicians for reassurance and care is a textbook illustration of dependent traits layered on top of (or entangled with) her delusional disorder. Worth confirming against your own lecture notes if you want the exact framing he used.

Section 12 · Cluster C

Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (OCPD) ⭐ HY

OCPD

"Type A personality"; "anal-retentive"
Core pictureInflexible, rigid striving for perfection — to the point that projects and tasks can't be completed on time because they're never "perfect enough." Preoccupation with details, rules, lists, and organization can become invasive enough to damage interpersonal functioning.

Mnemonic: LOW MIRTH

LetterCriterion
LLeisure activity is minimal
OOrganizational focus
WWork and productivity predominate
MMiserly spending habits
IInflexible around morals, values, etc.
RRigidity and stubbornness
TTask completion impaired (by perfectionism)
HHoards items — cannot discard them

OCD vs. OCPD — "Almost the Same Name, Almost Unrelated Conditions" ⭐ HY board favorite

🎙️
"Later on we're going to talk about obsessive-compulsive personality disorder, and the differences between OCD and OCPD — they couldn't be more unrelated, even though they have almost the same name. This is very commonly tested, because it's something a lot of people don't know the difference between."
OCDOCPD
Obsessions/compulsions?Yes — defining feature; ≥1 hour/day or significant impairmentNo — despite the name, OCPD has no true obsessions or compulsions at all
Ego orientationEgo-dystonic — bothersome, patient wants it to stopEgo-syntonic — consistent with self-image, no insight, not bothered by it
CategoryOCD & Related Disorders chapter (an anxiety-spectrum condition)Personality disorder (Cluster C)

Cluster C Summary

All three Cluster C disorders share an underlying anxious symptomatology — avoidant is "inhibited," dependent is "insecure," OCPD is "rigid, requiring order"

Section 13

Treatment ⭐ HY

⚠️
The single most important fact in this entire topic: THERE IS NO FDA-APPROVED MEDICATION TO TREAT ANY PERSONALITY DISORDER — not one, for any of the 10. Any medication used is off-label, targeting symptoms that arise from the disorder (depression, paranoia, irritability, affective instability) rather than the core disorder itself.

Borderline PD: The Exception Worth Knowing

Evidence for pharmacotherapy in BPD specifically is weak, but polypharmacy is extremely common in practice
>50% of BPD patients are on 2 psychotropic medications
>11% are on 5+ psychotropics simultaneously
Quetiapine has shown significant improvement on the Zanarini Rating Scale for BPD — 82% response vs. 48% placebo
APA recommends medication as adjunctive treatment for specific symptom domains: affective instability, impulsivity, psychosis, self-destructive behavior — never as monotherapy for the disorder itself

Psychotherapy Is the Real Mainstay

💡
For every personality disorder besides BPD, psychotherapy is the primary treatment, sometimes continued alongside symptom-targeted medication. Drugs are explicitly not cost-effective substitutes for behavioral psychotherapy.

DBT's four modules, each targeting one of BPD's core dysregulation domains: core mindfulness (cognitive dysregulation), distress tolerance (impulsiveness), emotion regulation (labile moods/emotions), interpersonal effectiveness (interpersonal chaos)

🧠
The exam shortcut: DBT (dialectical behavioral therapy) is specifically for borderline PD; CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) is the mainstay for the other 9 personality disorders. Dr. Smith's exact framing: "DBT is a form of CBT, so if the exam has DBT as an option, choose it; if not, choose CBT." In other words, DBT beats CBT as an answer choice only when the vignette is specifically about BPD — otherwise, default to CBT.
Section 14

Humorous Allegory: The Parking Lot of the Personality Disordered

A genuinely useful (and memorable) way to hold all 10 — plus a bonus 11th — disorders in your head at once, mapped onto a single, familiar scenario: parking a car.

Each parking spot/behavior maps to a personality disorder's core trait

Paranoid — "Cornered again!"
Narcissist — largest car, prominent hood ornament
Dependent — needs other cars to feel sheltered
Passive-aggressive — angles the car to take up 2 spaces
Borderline — rams into the car of an ex
Antisocial — blocks other cars in
Histrionic — parks in the center of the lot for dramatic effect
Obsessive-compulsive — perfect alignment in the parking space
Avoidant — hides in a corner
Schizoid — can't tolerate closeness to other cars
Schizotypal — parked in intergalactic parking (off in its own world)
💡
Passive-aggressive personality disorder — not one of the 10 official DSM-5 personality disorders (it was moved to the DSM-5 appendix as a condition needing further study, having appeared in earlier DSM editions), but it's a useful concept and shows up in this mnemonic since it's still occasionally referenced clinically and colloquially.
Section 15

Practice Questions — "What's the Most Likely Diagnosis?"

Per Dr. Smith: nearly all boards questions on this topic are first-order diagnosis questions. Tap an option to check your answer.

Question 1
A 44-year-old man believes his coworkers are constantly plotting against him, despite no evidence. He confides in no one at work, has ended several friendships over perceived slights he still resents years later, and repeatedly accuses his wife of infidelity despite her consistent whereabouts being verifiable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Paranoid personality disorder
B. Delusional disorder, jealous type
C. Schizotypal personality disorder
D. Paranoid schizophrenia
Answer: A. Grudges held long-term, doubting trustworthiness, and questioning a partner's fidelity without basis are classic GET FACT criteria (Section 03) — pervasive across relationships, not one encapsulated delusion (which would favor B), and with no hallucinations/disorganization to suggest schizophrenia (D).
Question 2
A 38-year-old night security guard lives alone, has never married, and reports no close friends. When told he is being considered for a promotion with more public interaction, he responds flatly, "That's fine," with no visible enthusiasm or concern either way. He denies feeling isolated or unhappy with his life. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Avoidant personality disorder
B. Schizoid personality disorder
C. Major depressive disorder
D. Schizotypal personality disorder
Answer: B. Solitary lifestyle, indifference to praise/criticism (the flat "that's fine"), and genuine contentment with isolation — not fear-driven avoidance (A) — is textbook schizoid PD (Section 04). No depressed mood or anhedonia is described to support C.
Question 3
A 29-year-old woman believes she can predict rainfall by reading patterns in her tea leaves. She dresses eccentrically and has no friends outside her sister. She finds ordinary interactions with cashiers or coworkers deeply uncomfortable, but denies feeling that anything is wrong with how she looks or comes across to others. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Schizoid personality disorder
B. Avoidant personality disorder
C. Schizotypal personality disorder
D. Brief psychotic disorder
Answer: C. Unusual perceptions/magical thinking (tea-leaf clairvoyance), eccentric appearance, and discomfort with interaction driven by the act of interacting — not negative self-image (ruling out avoidant, B) — is the schizotypal picture (UFO AIDER, Section 05). No frank psychosis/timeline criteria are described to support D.
Question 4
A 24-year-old man has a documented history of juvenile arrests for theft and animal cruelty beginning at age 12. He shows no remorse for repeatedly stealing from his roommate, has an unstable work history, and has been aggressive toward multiple partners. What additional historical criterion is required to formally diagnose him with antisocial personality disorder?
A. Documented conduct disorder before age 15
B. A prior suicide attempt
C. A formal diagnosis of ADHD in childhood
D. Evidence of a psychotic episode
Answer: A. Antisocial PD is one of the only personality disorders with an explicit childhood-onset prerequisite built into the criteria — conduct disorder before age 15, plus current age ≥18 (CALLOUS MAN, Section 06). His juvenile theft/animal cruelty history already suggests this was likely present.
Question 5
A 26-year-old woman describes a new therapist as "the only person who has ever truly understood me." Six weeks later she calls the same therapist "worthless, just like everyone else" after a scheduling conflict. She reports cutting her forearms "to feel something real" and describes intense terror at the idea of being alone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Bipolar I disorder
B. Borderline personality disorder
C. Histrionic personality disorder
D. Major depressive disorder, recurrent
Answer: B. Idealization-then-devaluation ("splitting"), self-harm aimed at feeling physical rather than emotional pain (para-suicidal behavior, not true suicidality), and frantic fear of abandonment are the I RAISED A PAIN criteria (Section 07). The rapid, interpersonally-triggered shift (weeks, tied to a specific relational event) favors BPD over a bipolar mood episode (A).
Question 6
Which feature most reliably distinguishes borderline personality disorder's affective instability from a bipolar mood episode?
A. BPD mood shifts always last several weeks, just like bipolar episodes
B. BPD mood shifts are rapid and reactive to interpersonal triggers, embedded in a broader pattern of relationship instability and identity disturbance
C. Bipolar disorder is ego-syntonic, while BPD is ego-dystonic
D. Only bipolar disorder can involve self-harm
Answer: B. BPD and bipolar disorder are classically confused in both directions (Section 07) — the key discriminator is that BPD's mood instability is fast (hours), reactive to specific relational triggers (fear of abandonment, a perceived slight), and sits inside a broader personality pattern, rather than existing as an autonomous, sustained mood episode.
Question 7
A 33-year-old woman arrives to every appointment in dramatic, provocative clothing. She describes a minor cold as "honestly the worst thing that has ever happened to me," flirts openly with the physician, and her displayed distress resolves within minutes once the conversation moves elsewhere. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Narcissistic personality disorder
B. Histrionic personality disorder
C. Borderline personality disorder
D. Somatic symptom disorder
Answer: B. Provocative presentation, theatrical/exaggerated but shallow and rapidly-shifting emotional displays, and a need to be the center of attention are the I CRAVE SIN criteria (Section 08) — distinguished from narcissism (A) by the attention-seeking being about emotional drama/appearance rather than grandiosity/superiority.
Question 8
A surgeon insists on being introduced as "the best in the state" at every conference, dismisses his colleagues' research as inferior, and becomes visibly enraged when a resident receives an award instead of him. He shows little concern for a patient's complaint about a long wait time, redirecting the conversation to his own accomplishments. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Antisocial personality disorder
B. Histrionic personality disorder
C. Narcissistic personality disorder
D. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
Answer: C. Grandiosity, need for admiration, envy of others' recognition, and lack of empathy are the A FAME GAME criteria (Section 09) — distinguished from antisocial PD (A) by the absence of rule-breaking/rights violations, and from histrionic (B) by the focus being on status/superiority rather than emotional drama.
Question 9
A man says he genuinely wants close friendships and a promotion at work, but repeatedly turns down both a coworker's invitation to socialize and a management role requiring more team interaction, fearing he will embarrass himself and be laughed at. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Schizoid personality disorder
B. Avoidant personality disorder
C. Social anxiety disorder
D. Dependent personality disorder
Answer: B. The explicit desire for connection, paired with avoidance driven by fear of ridicule/embarrassment (not indifference), is the RIDICULE pattern (Section 10) — the key differentiator from schizoid PD (A), which lacks any real desire for relationships in the first place. (Social anxiety disorder, C, is a reasonable distractor, but the pervasive, trait-level, lifelong pattern across both social and occupational domains points to a personality disorder rather than an anxiety disorder confined to specific performance/social situations.)
Question 10
A 41-year-old woman cannot decide what to order at a restaurant without calling her sister first. She began dating someone new one week after her last relationship ended, stating she "can't be alone." She has allowed her partner to manage all of her finances and medical appointments for over a decade. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Borderline personality disorder
B. Dependent personality disorder
C. Avoidant personality disorder
D. Histrionic personality disorder
Answer: B. Difficulty with independent decisions, delegating major responsibilities, rapid rebound into new relationships to avoid being alone — the DARN HURT criteria (Section 11). Unlike BPD (A), there's no splitting/idealization-devaluation or self-harm described — just a stable, longstanding pattern of excessive reliance on others.
Question 11
An accountant has not taken a vacation in 10 years and routinely misses project deadlines because he insists on triple-checking every entry until it's "perfect." He is rigid about the one correct way to file documents and becomes irritated when others don't follow his system. He sees nothing unusual about any of this and believes his colleagues are simply careless. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Obsessive-compulsive disorder
B. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
C. Generalized anxiety disorder
D. Narcissistic personality disorder
Answer: B. No true obsessions or compulsions are described — this is rigidity, perfectionism, and a productivity/organization focus that's ego-syntonic (he sees nothing wrong; he blames others) — the LOW MIRTH picture (Section 12). True OCD (A) would require actual obsessions/compulsions and would be ego-dystonic, with the patient distressed by his own behavior.
Question 12
A 24-year-old woman meets full criteria for borderline personality disorder, including recurrent self-harm and highly unstable relationships. Which specific psychotherapy modality is most appropriate as first-line treatment?
A. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)
B. Dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT)
C. Psychoanalysis
D. Exposure and response prevention
Answer: B. DBT was developed specifically for BPD and is the only personality disorder with a dedicated first-line psychotherapy (Section 13). Remember the exam shortcut: DBT is technically a form of CBT — "if DBT is an option, choose it; if not, choose CBT" — but when both are listed and the vignette is BPD, DBT is the more specific and correct answer.
Section 16

Rapid Review Grid

Trait vs. Disorder
Everyone has traits. A disorder = a cluster of traits causing real, pervasive impairment.
3 defining words
Pervasive (all areas of life), inflexible (hard to change), maladaptive (against social norms).
Ego-syntonic
No conflict with self-view; no insight; "the world is the problem, not me." Rarely self-presents.
Onset
Traceable to adolescence or earlier — never truly develops fresh in mid-adulthood (can be missed until then).
3 clusters
A = Weird/eccentric. B = Wild/dramatic. C = Worried/anxious.
Cluster A
Paranoid (GET FACT), Schizoid (SIR SAFE), Schizotypal (UFO AIDER) — share negative symptoms of schizophrenia.
Cluster B
Antisocial (CALLOUS MAN), Borderline (I RAISED A PAIN), Histrionic (I CRAVE SIN), Narcissistic (A FAME GAME).
Cluster C
Avoidant (RIDICULE), Dependent (DARN HURT), OCPD (LOW MIRTH) — share anxious symptomatology.
Schizoid vs. Avoidant
Schizoid = doesn't want relationships. Avoidant = wants them, but fears rejection.
Schizotypal's signature
Unusual perceptions/magical thinking; NOT driven by negative self-image; most linked to true psychosis.
Antisocial's prerequisite
Documented conduct disorder before age 15 + current age ≥18.
BPD self-harm
About physical pain distracting from emotional pain, NOT suicidal intent — "para-suicidal."
BPD vs. Bipolar
BPD = rapid, reactive, interpersonally-triggered mood shifts. Bipolar = sustained, autonomous episodes.
BPD name origin
"Borderline" of depression and psychosis — can have micropsychotic/dissociative episodes under stress.
Histrionic vs. Narcissistic
Histrionic = center of attention via emotional drama. Narcissistic = center of attention via grandiosity/superiority.
OCD vs. OCPD
OCD = true obsessions/compulsions, ego-dystonic, anxiety-spectrum. OCPD = NO true obsessions/compulsions, ego-syntonic, personality disorder.
No FDA-approved meds
Zero, for any of the 10 personality disorders. All pharmacotherapy is off-label, symptom-targeted.
BPD polypharmacy
>50% on 2 psychotropics; >11% on 5+. Quetiapine: 82% response vs. 48% placebo on Zanarini scale.
Psychotherapy rule
DBT specifically for BPD; CBT for the other 9. "If DBT's an option, choose it; if not, choose CBT."

⭐ High-Yield One-Pager

Personality Disorders — condensed pre-exam summary

Foundations

  • Trait = normal variation. Disorder = pervasive + inflexible + maladaptive cluster of traits
  • Ego-syntonic: no insight, "world is the problem not me," rarely self-presents
  • Onset traceable to adolescence or earlier — never develops fresh mid-life
  • Diagnosis often requires collateral history (spouse/family confirming lifelong pattern)

3 Clusters

  • A = "Weird" (odd/eccentric): Paranoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal — share negative sx of schizophrenia
  • B = "Wild" (dramatic/erratic): Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic
  • C = "Worried" (anxious/fearful): Avoidant, Dependent, OCPD — share anxious symptomatology

Cluster A Mnemonics

  • Paranoid — GET FACT (grudges, exploitation, trust doubted, fidelity questioned, attacks perceived, confides rarely, threats read in)
  • Schizoid — SIR SAFE (solitary, indifferent, relationships/sex/activities/friends lacking, emotionally cold)
  • Schizotypal — UFO AIDER (unusual perceptions, friendless, odd beliefs, affect odd, ideas of reference, doubts others, eccentric, reluctant)

Cluster B Mnemonics

  • Antisocial — CALLOUS MAN (conduct d/o <15, arrests, lies, no superego, obligations unmet, unstable, unsafe, money problems, aggressive)
  • Borderline — I RAISED A PAIN (identity, relationships unstable, abandonment avoided, impulsive, suicidal gestures, empty, dissociative, affect unstable, paranoid ideation, anger, idealize/devalue, negativistic)
  • Histrionic — I CRAVE SIN (inappropriate/seductive, center of attention, relationships overestimated, appearance-focused, vulnerable to suggestion, exaggerated emotion, shifting/shallow, impressionistic speech, novelty craved)
  • Narcissistic — A FAME GAME (admiration, fantasizes success, arrogant, manipulative, envious, grandiose, associates w/ special people, me-first, empathy lacking)

Cluster C Mnemonics

  • Avoidant — RIDICULE (restrained, inhibited, disapproval expected, inadequate self-view, criticism expected, unwilling to get involved, longs for attachment, embarrassment feared)
  • Dependent — DARN HURT (disagreement hard, advice needed, responsibility delegated, nurturance sought, helpless alone, unrealistic self-care worry, relationships desperately sought, tasks hard to initiate)
  • OCPD — LOW MIRTH (leisure minimal, organization focus, work predominates, miserly, inflexible morals, rigid/stubborn, task completion impaired, hoards)

Key Differentiators

  • Schizoid (doesn't want relationships) vs. Avoidant (wants them, fears rejection)
  • OCD (true obsessions/compulsions, ego-dystonic) vs. OCPD (none, ego-syntonic)
  • BPD (rapid/reactive mood shifts, interpersonal triggers) vs. Bipolar (sustained autonomous episodes)
  • Histrionic (drama/attention) vs. Narcissistic (grandiosity/superiority)

Borderline PD Specifics

  • Name = "borderline" of depression and psychosis; micropsychotic/dissociative episodes under stress
  • Self-harm = para-suicidal (physical pain distracts from emotional pain), NOT usually suicidal intent
  • Ask: "Do you feel empty inside?" — classic affirmative response
  • Splitting: idealization → devaluation, black/white relationship view

Antisocial PD Specifics

  • = Sociopathy / psychopathy (lay terms)
  • REQUIRES documented conduct disorder before age 15 + current age ≥18
  • No superego; no remorse; externalizes all blame

Treatment

  • NO FDA-approved medication for ANY of the 10 personality disorders
  • DBT = specifically for BPD; CBT = mainstay for the other 9
  • "If DBT's an option, choose it; if not, choose CBT"
  • BPD polypharmacy: >50% on 2 psychotropics, >11% on 5+; quetiapine 82% vs 48% placebo response (Zanarini scale)
  • Meds target symptoms (depression, irritability, psychosis) — never the core disorder itself

All 10 at a Glance

  • Paranoid: distrust, malicious-motive assumption, grudges
  • Schizoid: genuinely prefers solitude, blunted affect
  • Schizotypal: unusual perceptions, magical thinking, odd speech
  • Antisocial: disregards rights of others, no remorse, conduct d/o hx
  • Borderline: unstable identity/relationships, abandonment fear, self-harm
  • Histrionic: attention-seeking, theatrical, shallow/shifting emotion
  • Narcissistic: grandiosity, entitlement, lacks empathy
  • Avoidant: wants relationships but fears rejection/ridicule
  • Dependent: clingy, needs excessive care/reassurance, indecisive
  • OCPD: rigid perfectionism, no true obsessions/compulsions, ego-syntonic

Built from Ryan Smith, DO, PhD's "Personality Disorders 2026" — UNE COM OMS-1 Psychiatry Block.
